description_ru: На собеседовании на должность куратора музея соискателю задают неудобные вопросы о спорных экспонатах, бюджете и сопротивлении системы.
text:
Dr Whitcombe: Thank you for coming, Mr Lindqvist, and for applying for the post of curator. Do sit. I'm Dr Whitcombe, this is Ms Adeyemi from our education team, and you've already met the very patient gentleman at reception.
Sam: I have, and he gave me excellent advice. He said the panel always asks the same three questions, and that I should ignore my prepared answers.
Ms Adeyemi: Did he really? I shall have a word. In that case, we'll have to be inventive. Let's start with something different. If you could remove one object from our collection, which would it be?

Sam: Remove it, as in destroy it, or as in return it somewhere?
Dr Whitcombe: Interesting that you ask. Either. Choose.
Sam: Then I'd choose the bronze figure in Gallery Four, the one labelled "Court Official, probably nineteenth century." Your own file notes admit that its provenance is uncertain. I'd want to find out whether it was taken legitimately, and if it wasn't, I'd arrange its return. It might leave a gap on the plinth, but a gap with an honest label is more truthful than a beautiful object with a doubtful past.

Ms Adeyemi: That's rather bold for a first answer. Dr Whitcombe has spent six years defending that figure.
Dr Whitcombe: I have. And I'd prefer you didn't look quite so pleased with yourself.
Sam: I'm sorry. I wasn't aware of the history. I wouldn't have put it so bluntly.

Dr Whitcombe: No, no, please. I asked, and you answered. The remarkable thing is that nobody else on the shortlist even noticed the label. Let's go on. Tell me about a time an exhibition you worked on went badly.
Sam: Last year, at the maritime museum, we mounted a show on shipwrecks. We were very proud of it. Dramatic lighting, recorded wind, a fog machine. And then a woman in her seventies stopped in front of the case containing a child's shoe, which had been recovered from a wreck, and began to cry. Her grandmother's family had been aboard.
Ms Adeyemi: How did you respond?

Sam: At the time, badly. I told a colleague we should put up a warning sign. He said that would be patronising, and I said it would be considerate, and we argued for ten minutes while she stood there. Eventually, a young volunteer simply went and sat beside her, and asked about her grandmother. Within an hour, she was telling stories to a small crowd of strangers.
Dr Whitcombe: And what did you learn from that?
Sam: That we had designed the exhibition around the objects, and forgotten the visitors who might arrive with objects of their own. Afterwards we added a quiet room with a notebook, and invited people to write down their own family stories. We now have more than four hundred entries, and I consider it the best thing we ever made.

Dr Whitcombe: Did the museum change anything permanent as a result, or was it a one-off gesture?
Sam: Both, honestly. The director resisted at first, because she feared the notebook would become a place for complaints. For the first month it was almost empty. Then a schoolboy wrote three lines about his father's fishing boat, and after that people queued to write.

Ms Adeyemi: That's a lovely answer, if you'll forgive the word. But let me be sceptical. Museums are under enormous financial pressure. We can't all build quiet rooms with notebooks. What would you cut?
Sam: I'd cut the fog machine, for a start. Joking aside, I'd rather have fewer, better-researched exhibitions than a constant churn of spectacle. Visitors can sense when something has been made to impress them, rather than to speak to them. But I'd also be honest that this has a cost. Fewer blockbusters usually means fewer tickets.
Ms Adeyemi: And the staff? Cutting spectacle tends to make designers nervous.

Sam: It should make them excited, if you frame it correctly. A restrained exhibition is far harder to design than a noisy one, because there's nowhere to hide. I'd involve the designers at the very beginning, not hand them a finished script and ask them to decorate it.
Dr Whitcombe: So how would you pay for it?
Sam: Partly through partnerships with schools and universities, who have the researchers and the need for real objects. And partly by being candid with funders. In my experience, they respond much better to "here's what we've learned" than to "here's a glossy report about how well everything went."

Ms Adeyemi: Hmm. Funders do like glossy reports.
Sam: They do, but they also like not being deceived, and eventually they notice the difference.
Dr Whitcombe: Let me ask you the final question, and it is a little personal. This is a large institution, with very strong opinions and a certain amount of inertia. You would be the youngest member of the senior team. What happens the first time somebody senior tells you that an idea of yours is impractical?

Sam: I'd ask them to explain why, and I'd listen. If they're right, I'd say so. If they're wrong, I'd ask what evidence would change their mind, and I'd go and get it. And if I still failed, I'd wait. I've found that institutions are slower than people but, over time, rather more reasonable.
Ms Adeyemi: That's either very wise or very diplomatic.
Sam: I'm hoping the two are not mutually exclusive.

Dr Whitcombe: Thank you, Mr Lindqvist. We'll be in touch by Friday. Oh, and one last thing. About the bronze figure.
Sam: Yes?
Dr Whitcombe: I've been looking at that file again this week, in spite of myself. Don't tell Ms Adeyemi, but I think you may be right.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˈprovenance, leˈgitimately, inˈertia. В legitimately второй слог ударный, остальные коротко.
В конце слова plinth сочетание «nθ»: язык между зубами, глухо; не заканчивайте на «т».
Безударные слоги сокращайте до «ə»: museum, collection, visitors звучат с очень краткой серединой.
В начале ударного слога p, t, k придыхательные: colleague, patronising.

questions.question: Which object would Sam remove from the collection?
questions.answer: The bronze figure in Gallery Four, because its provenance is doubtful.

questions.question: What went wrong in the shipwreck exhibition?
questions.answer: A visitor cried at a child's shoe from a wreck her family had been on, and the staff were unprepared.

questions.question: What did Sam's museum add afterwards?
questions.answer: A quiet room with a notebook where visitors write family stories.

questions.question: What does Dr Whitcombe admit at the end?
questions.answer: That Sam may be right about the bronze figure.
